lines.text: Between the Atlas Mountains, the Sahara and two seas lies a kingdom of old dynasties and older cities. This is the story of Morocco.
The story of Morocco reaches back further than most. At Jebel Irhoud, fossils about three hundred thousand years old are the oldest known of our own species.
Much later, a city grew at Volubilis in the north, which under Rome became a busy outpost of the empire. Its ruins still stand among the olive groves.
In 788 Idris, a descendant of the Prophet, founded the first Muslim dynasty of Morocco.
From the Idrisids, Morocco dates its long line of kingdoms, a royal tradition that reaches across more than twelve centuries.
Idris also founded Fez, which would become the old capital and a great centre of learning.
There, in 859, a woman named Fatima al-Fihri founded al-Qarawiyyin, often called the oldest working university in the world.
In the eleventh century, Berber warriors from the Sahara, the Almoravids, swept north and ruled both Morocco and Muslim Spain.
They founded a new capital, Marrakesh, the red city, whose name would give the country its name in many languages.
The Almohads followed, another Berber empire, ruling from Marrakesh to Seville, building the Giralda and sheltering scholars such as Averroes.
In Marrakesh they built the Koutoubia Mosque, whose tall minaret became a model for others.
In 1304 Ibn Battuta was born in Tangier. He would spend about thirty years travelling from West Africa to China and tell of it all in his book.
In 1471 the mountain town of Chefchaouen was founded in the Rif, a place now famous for its houses painted blue.
In 1666 the Alaouites took the throne. Their family still reigns, and kept Morocco free of Ottoman rule.
In 1912 that freedom was lost. France made most of Morocco a protectorate, and Spain took the north.
In 1921 the Berbers of the Rif rose under Abd el-Krim, defeating Spain before France and Spain together crushed the revolt.
In 1929 the future Hassan the Second was born. As king he would rule with an iron hand, in what Moroccans call the years of lead.
His son, Mohammed the Sixth, born in 1963, would succeed him in 1999.
Independence came in 1956. Then in 1975, some three hundred and fifty thousand Moroccans marched into Western Sahara in the Green March.
In 1993 the Hassan the Second Mosque was finished on the sea at Casablanca, with one of the tallest minarets in the world.
And in September 2023 an earthquake struck the High Atlas near Marrakesh, killing nearly three thousand people.
From the first humans to the old medinas, Morocco keeps its long past close at hand.
